concepts.gloss: A recognised item of vocabulary known conventionally to speakers, not merely an output of an available productive rule.
A word conforming to current word-formation rules that has not become established, regardless of whether it has ever been used.
A non-established word actually used on an occasion; a subset of potential words where the form is well formed.
Conformity to the rules of present-day English word-formation, distinct from lexical establishment and stylistic approval.
Conventional recognition of a word as part of vocabulary, as distinct from its formal morphological admissibility.
Conditions restricting which novel word forms can be produced by currently available morphological processes.
A subjective reaction to the elegance or suitability of a proposed new word, distinct from its structural well-formedness.
A productive verb-to-adjective -able step followed by an adjective-to-noun nominalization with -ity.
An inherited suffixation pattern present in established words but no longer available for ordinary creation of novel Present-day English words.
An inherited agent-forming compound type made from plain verb and its direct-object noun, no longer productive for new words.
Retention of established words despite the loss of productivity of their original formation processes.
The distinction between dictionaries' entries, including idiomatic multiword expressions, and the larger set of grammatical established and potential words.

rules.statement: An established word is recognised by speakers as an individual vocabulary item; it can have an idiosyncratic or historically inherited formation that need not be available for making new words.
rules.condition: Classify a lexical item as established when it is conventionally familiar in the language, rather than merely matching a productive construction; an established form can remain usable even when the process that first produced it has ceased to be productive.

contrast.text: The museum has an exhibit about the medieval bishopric. [bishopric is an established lexical item, not a productive model for new -ric formations]
The kingdom's eastern border followed the river. [kingdom is an established lexical item]
The editor praised the writer's unfaithfulness to a restrictive style guide. [a conventionally available lexical item]
The speaker proposed a novel expression during the workshop. [coinage alone does not demonstrate establishment]

rules.statement: A potential word is a non-established word whose formation accords with Present-day English word-formation rules, whether or not anyone has previously used it.
rules.condition: For a proposed lexical word that is not already part of the established vocabulary, classify it as potential if it is morphologically admissible under an available word-formation process, without requiring prior attestation or a dictionary entry.

An established word is not reclassified as merely potential every time a speaker invents a new use for it. [establishment is a separate property]

rules.statement: A nonce-word has been used on an occasion but has not become established, while the larger class of potential words also includes well-formed coinages that have never been used.
rules.condition: When a morphologically admissible word is non-established, record whether it has actually been used: attested ad-hoc use makes it a nonce-word, whereas mere possible formation still qualifies it as a potential word; use alone does not establish permanent vocabulary status.

rules.concept: stylistic preference distinguished from morphological grammaticality
rules.statement: A morphologically well-formed new word may be criticised for awkward style, but stylistic dislike does not by itself make the word ill-formed under word-formation rules.
rules.condition: For a proposed lexical word created by a currently available English formation process, evaluate morphological licensing separately from whether particular speakers find the word elegant or idiomatic.

The editorial team replaced a complex noun with a plain phrase for readability. [an editing choice does not imply ungrammaticality]

rules.statement: A verb can form an adjective with the productive suffix -able, and that adjective can form a noun with -ity, with a change in the ending, to express a property of the original action.
rules.condition: For a verb that licenses -able, analyse a derived nominal such as repairability as an adjective stage in -able followed by noun-forming -ity, taking account of the -able to -ability shape; do not assume every verb must allow this derivation.

exceptions.description: The two-step pattern is available only where the verb supports the adjective-forming -able derivation; the subsection does not license it indiscriminately for all verbs.

rules.concept: nonproductive -ric formation in established lexical words
rules.statement: The old -ric suffix survives in established lexical items but is not a productive Present-day English device for coining words for new jurisdictions or offices.
rules.condition: When a newly proposed noun is modelled by attaching -ric to a title as in an inherited established form such as bishopric, distinguish the historical established lexical item from the unsupported attempt to extend that suffix as an ordinary productive present-day pattern.

exceptions.description: Established words formed by the inherited pattern remain established vocabulary even when their formative process is no longer productive.

rules.statement: The inherited agent-denoting compound pattern with a plain-form verb followed by its direct-object noun is no longer generally available for freely coining new Present-day English words, although established historical instances remain.
rules.condition: For an intended new agent noun formed as a bare verb followed by the noun denoting its direct object, distinguish historical established compounds such as pickpocket from a novel attempt to apply the same inherited agent-word pattern; do not confuse this with all productive verb-noun compounding.

exceptions.description: Established historical words exemplifying the unavailable formation pattern remain valid lexical items.

rules.concept: dictionary inventories versus grammatical word inventories
rules.statement: The inventory of dictionary entries differs from the inventory of grammatical words: dictionaries include multiword expressions and need not list every well-formed non-established word.
rules.condition: When comparing dictionary coverage with word status, treat lexicalised multiword dictionary entries as distinct from single grammatical words, and recognise morphologically admissible potential words even if absent from dictionary headword lists.

A novel form can be discussed in a grammar without being listed as an established dictionary item. [distinct purposes of grammar and dictionary]
